posts.hook: “It’s an easy fit, my brother-in-law said.”
posts.body:
“It’s an easy fit.”

Three words that have ended more window careers than any health and safety course.

The brother-in-law has never touched a reveal. The brother-in-law does not know the cavity is 40mm short of the frame. The brother-in-law has never had to scribe a 6mm wedge into a brick corner while a customer watches from a Velux.

Easiest job in the world. Ten out of ten.

posts.hook: “The wall is straight.” It is not.
posts.body:
The reveal said 70mm.
The reveal measured 52mm.
The reveal is 70mm at the top and 52mm at the bottom and 61mm in the middle, because of course it is.

The client told me three times the wall was straight. The client was standing in front of the wall. The client could not see the wall.

The wall is a 1920s extension, built by a man who was very keen on doing things his own way.

posts.hook: The reveal is fine. The reveal is always fine. The problem is above it.
posts.body:
Nobody looks up.

Customer looks at the wall. Fitter looks at the reveal. Surveyor looks at the reveal. Office looks at the spreadsheet. Everyone agrees the reveal is fine.

Meanwhile the lintel is 12mm out of level, the cavity is full of 1980s expanding foam, and there is a cast iron soil pipe sitting exactly where the frame needs to go.

The window was never the problem.

posts.hook: “We’re just out of…” and then silence
posts.body:
“We’re just out of white silicone.”

I say it. Every single fitter has said it. Somewhere in a van on the M4 there is a tube of white silicone and there will be until Thursday.

You look at the tube. You look at the bead. You look at the tube again. You squeeze. Nothing. You look at the date. 2019.

The job does not stop. You clear the joint, mask it, fit it, and hope.

posts.hook: The variation landed in the office, the job left the workshop.
posts.body:
This is the one that keeps me up.

Survey says the opening is 4mm different. Surveyor photographs it, notes it, and flags the variation on his phone. Meanwhile the office has already released the job, the workshop has already cut, and the frame is on a van.

The photo was in a WhatsApp group. Nobody was in the WhatsApp group. The surveyor was in Fenora. The office was in a spreadsheet.

Same job. Two systems. One remake.

The photo was in a WhatsApp group. Nobody was in the WhatsApp group. The surveyor was in Fenora. The office was in a spreadsheet.

Same job. Two systems. One remake.

This is the problem Fenora exists to kill. Link in bio.

posts.hook: My least favourite four words in the English language.
posts.body:
“Is it meant to do that?”

You are 40 minutes into a fitting. The room is upside down. There is foam on the floor and a vacuum cleaner that stopped working in 2011.

“Will it stop doing that when the glass is in?”

No. It will stop doing that when I shim the bottom corner. Give me nine minutes.

“You’ve got nine minutes?”

I do not.

posts.hook: Priced 14. Yesterday I said 11. Today I say 13.
posts.body:
Scope it yourself and you can move the price all day long.

Monday: £11,000.
Tuesday: £14,000 — “we forgot the french doors.”
Wednesday: £9,500 — “it’s an easy fit.”
Thursday: £13,000 — “I’ve had a cheaper one.”
Friday: £10,000 — “that first quote was a mistake, make it 11.”

Monday: £10,000.

Nobody in this trade believes a number until three people have quoted a different one.

posts.hook: “I’ve watched a video.”
posts.body:
Customer has watched eleven videos.

Customer now knows that the industry standard is to fit with 8mm of closed-cell foam behind the frame. Customer believes the frame should be screwed into the brick. Customer has opinions about the gap.

Customer is not wrong about the foam. Customer is about to be very wrong about the brick.

There is no coming back from “I’ve watched a video.”

posts.hook: Every job ever, ranked by how long the customer said it would take
posts.body:
How long they said: two days.
How long the job is: eleven weeks of drip-by-drip decisions.

Day 1 they choose the glass.
Day 4 they change the glass.
Day 9 they change the colour.
Day 12 they want the colour to match the door, not the door to match the window.
Day 30 they ask if it can be in eggshell.

It cannot be in eggshell.

posts.hook: Old frames come out. The hole is worse than you thought.
posts.body:
The best bit of every window job is the moment the old frame comes out and the hole is just a rectangular hole in a wall.

For about nine seconds, the job is easy.

Then you see the sill, the lintel, the reveals, the three different DPCs laid by three different builders, and a length of lead pipe that goes nowhere.

There is always a dog.

And there is always a moment — usually ten minutes in — when the dog decides this is now their job.

You cannot move a Labrador. You have tried. Everyone has tried.

posts.hook: It’s not level. I told you it wasn’t level.
posts.body:
Hour 4, the bottom corner is 6mm proud.

“I told you it wasn’t level.”

You did tell me. You told me in the first ten minutes. I wrote it down. I photographed it. I put it on the survey. I told the office. The office told the workshop. The workshop made it to the survey.

And then the survey got lost, because it was in a different system, and nobody checked.

So: it’s not level. You told me. Now can you help me shim it?

And then the survey got lost, because it was in a different system, and nobody checked.

So: it’s not level. You told me. Now can you help me shim it?

posts.hook: “Is it scratch or is it crack?” is not a customer question. It is a philosophy.
posts.body:
“There’s a mark on the glass.”

There is always a mark on the glass.

Sometimes it’s a scratch. Sometimes it’s a reflection of the sky. Sometimes it’s a bug that got in during the last rain and is now fused to the pane. Sometimes it’s the neighbour’s security light. Sometimes it’s been there since the day it was fitted and the customer is just now, at 9pm, noticing it for the first time in two years.

posts.hook: Rain on the day. Every time.
posts.body:
Survey in the rain. Fit on the day it pours. The one time you need it to be dry, it is 47mm of it and the render is soaking.

You fit wet. You foam wet. You seal wet. You know sealing wet is wrong. You do it anyway because the customer is going on holiday Friday and you have a good job doing.

In ten years that seal will fail and it will be entirely your fault and entirely the rain’s fault and entirely the client’s fault for booking it in November.

posts.hook: The payment. The actual hardest part of the job.
posts.body:
The job took nine days.
The job went brilliantly.
The customer was delighted. The customer sent a lovely message. The customer recommended us to two neighbours.

“It’ll go on the invoice.”

“It did go on the invoice.”

“When will it be paid.”

“I’ll check with the office.”

The office will check with the customer. The customer will check with the accountant. The accountant will check with the bank. The bank will send a notification that will not be read until 6pm on a Friday.

posts.hook: The apprentice says the thing you told him not to say.

“You’ve told him the job was two days, hasn’t you.”

Halfway through day one he is on the phone: “Yeah no, he says three to four days.”

Day four at 4pm: “He says it’s definitely done by six.”

Day six. The apprentice has moved on to a different job. I have not.

posts.hook: Sash windows. The sashes will drop.
posts.body:
Nobody mentions this at handover.

The sashes were fine for eleven years. The sashes were fine for twelve years. Then the ropes finally gave, the weights came down, and now it takes both hands and a good deal of swearing to get the top one up.

It was not going to last forever. You knew it was not going to last forever. You bought the house anyway. You paid for the house anyway.

That is what happens when you do not specify it. That is what happens when nobody asked what the cords are made of.

posts.hook: The three knocks before every delivery
posts.body:
You know the knock.

It’s not a knock, it’s a performance. Three knocks with intent. Wait for the reply. Knock again, two this time, slightly harder. Never call the bell — the bell is for pizza.

If nobody answers after the third round you have two options: leave, or stand in the rain looking like a person who has never been to a house before.

posts.hook: “It’s got a draught through it.” It has not.
posts.body:
“I’m getting a slight draught through the double glazing, you fitted it for me.”

It is 1mm of air moving past a closed sash in a house built in 1911 with a fireplace that is a permanent hole in the building.

You can do three things:
1. Explain why.
2. Offer to come back and adjust it, which will make it worse.
3. Leave a bag of cill wedges and a roll of brush sealer and explain that the fire is the draught.

Brian does a bit of everything.

Brian is not a fraud. Brian genuinely believes a draught excluder is a repair.

Brian has a very full diary and he will not be able to come back for six weeks.

posts.hook: There is a difference between “scribed” and “fudged”
posts.body:
Scribing is cutting the horn at an angle to follow the wall.

Fudging is cutting the horn at an angle and hoping the wall is what you thought it was.

They look identical from the outside. From the inside one is a joint line and one is a 6mm gap with a bead of silicone holding the world together.

The customer will find the difference. In eight years. On a Tuesday. Quietly.

posts.hook: Astragal ≠ astragal bar
posts.body:
Everybody in the trade knows somebody who calls it the wrong one and will not be corrected.

An astragal is the glazing bar itself — the timber or profile sitting between the panes.

An astragal bar is the metal or plastic insert that clips into it.

You can tell the difference by whether it makes a noise in the wind. If it does, you’ve got a bar and a gap.

posts.hook: Box sash vs spiral sash: the whole argument in one carousel
posts.body:
Slide 1: A box sash has ropes and weights in a box inside the jambs. The sashes sit 30–40mm apart. You can hear it move.

Slide 2: A spiral sash runs on a helix in a single track. The sashes sit 20–25mm apart. It is quieter, slimmer, and easier to seal.

Slide 3: The box looks better. Everyone in the room agrees the box looks better.

Slide 4: The spiral is what everyone actually wants fitted and no-one admits it.

posts.hook: Cill projection: the number nobody ever agrees on
posts.body:
65mm is standard.
75mm is better in the rain.
85mm is what your dad’s has got.

Then you get to the brickwork, and the brickwork has been repointed twice since 1974 and the face is now 12mm further out than the drawing, so your 65mm cill is now a 53mm cill, and now it is not standard and not better in the rain, it is just wet.

Standardise your cill projection. Write it on the job. Then argue about it once, in writing, forever.

posts.hook: Trickle vents. 5,000mm². Free air area. Per room.

The most unglamorous 25mm of plastic on the whole window and the one everybody forgets until Building Regs ask for the calcs.

A 2250mm² vent is a 2250mm² vent and it is not enough for a wet room and it is not enough for a new build and it is definitely not enough for the argument you are about to have.

Put the vent in the head, not the sill. Size it from the room, not from the catalogue.

Put it in the drawing so the installer doesn’t put it in the sill.

posts.hook: Georgian bars vs astragal bars vs faux glazing bars
posts.body:
Georgian bars: individual small panes, each one glazed, each one a weak point, each one expensive, each one a nightmare in a clean.

Astragal bars: fewer, thicker, glued to the inside face, cheaper, stronger, and from the street you genuinely cannot tell.

Faux bars: printed or applied to the glass. Looks perfect. Looks like a pub. Not for Grade II.

posts.hook: Glass build-up, in trade order
posts.body:
24mm, 6.12.4.2, argon, black spacer, warm edge, toughened, obscured.

Say it out loud in a customer meeting and watch their face. It is the same words as every other quote. It is not the same words.

What nobody writes down: whether the spacer is black, silver or warm edge. Whether the top pane is toughened. Whether the coated face is inside or out. Whether the calculator assumed a standard make-up when you specified a different one.

Four words on a quote. Four hours of argument later.

posts.hook: A “flush sash” is not flush and I need everyone to know
posts.body:
A flush casement is flush with the frame face.

That is it. That is the whole concept. The sash sits in the same plane as the outer frame.

What it is not: flush with the reveal. Flush with the wall. Flush with anything else. It is not flush with the architect’s rendering, and the customer will ask why the new window does not look like the drawing of the old house.

posts.hook: A bay is not a bay. It is a geometry.
posts.body:
A 45° canted bay loses about 30% of its glass to sightlines.

A 30° bay loses about 17%.

A 90° box gives you a structural pier in the middle of your living room wall.

Add a return on the end, add a door under it, add a monkey bar on top, and suddenly your “45 degree bay” is a bespoke fabrication with its own drawing, its own price and its own eight-week lead time.

It was always going to be bespoke. It was always going to have a drawing. Have the drawing before the customer picks the tile.

A 45° canted bay loses about 30% of its glass to sightlines.

A 30° bay loses about 17%.

A 90° box gives you a structural pier in the middle of your living room wall.

Add a return on the end, add a door under it, add a monkey bar on top, and suddenly your “45 degree bay” is a bespoke fabrication with its own drawing, its own price and its own eight-week lead time.

It was always going to be bespoke. It was always going to have a drawing. Have the drawing before the customer picks the tile.

posts.hook: Turn a corner: casement, tilt & turn, french, or all three?
posts.body:
Casement: cheapest, opens out, hinges eat clear glass.

Tilt & turn: opens in for cleaning, hinges invisible, hardware costs more.

French: two sashes, no mullion, doubles the sightline risk, best with a shallow reveal.

All three: a bifold, and now the lead time is six weeks and the hinge selection is the whole project.

Get this wrong on a ground floor rear elevation and someone is leaning out of a first floor window to clean it for the next fifteen years.

Glass area ≠ window area.

If you are comparing quotes on square metres of window, you are comparing sightlines, not daylight. Two identical 3.2m² windows can differ by 0.7m² of actual glass.

0.7m² of extra glass is worth more than the customer will ever say out loud, and it is completely invisible on your quote.

posts.hook: The 30-second window nerd test
posts.body:
Ask a window fitter these and watch their eyes light up:

1. What’s your cill projection?
2. Sash weight or rope and pulley?
3. What grade of stainless for the coastal job?
4. Is the glazing bar astragal or Georgian?
5. What’s your reveal tolerance?

If they answer all five without hesitating, hire them. If they say “it depends on the job”, they have never thought about it.

posts.hook: The dog-ear sill. Every job, every time, no exceptions.
posts.body:
There is a detail on almost every internal cill called the dog-ear — a small return at the end so the paint and the cill edge don’t meet in a horrible 90° corner that cracks on the first winter.

One small profile. It is on the drawing or it is not on the drawing. If it is not on the drawing, you will get a mitre.

Nobody has ever once wanted a mitre on a cill.

posts.hook: Fire and glazing. Nobody prices the hole.
posts.body:
The average UK living room fireplace with an open fire is a permanent 0.1m² hole in the building envelope.

No window specification on earth fixes that. Every window company in the country has quoted windows into a room with a fire in it and every one of those quotes implied a warmer room.

The honest conversation costs you the job sometimes. Do it anyway.

posts.hook: Presets: the most useful thing in your quote and the least used
posts.body:
A good preset is a window that is already right — a common size, a common spec, a known price, a known lead time, a known install time.

It turns a forty-minute quote into a ninety-second quote.
It turns “I’ll ring you back” into “done”.
It stops the office inventing a price at 6pm on a Friday.

If your most common window in your most common house is not a one-click preset, you are doing yourself harm.

No architrave is a cleaner modern detail.

No architrave is also: who is filling the gap between the frame and the plaster, and with what, and is that gap the same on all four sides, and is the plasterer coming back, and are they charging you for it.

“Flush fit” is not a finish. It is a conversation between three trades.

posts.hook: Your U-value is only as good as the edge
posts.body:
The middle of the glass is brilliant.
The edge of the frame is a thermal bridge with a marketing department.

The gap between the two is what the customer actually feels under their feet, and it is called the psi value, and it is the number that is missing from nine out of ten window quotes in this country.

Ask for the whole frame. Not the glass. The whole frame.

A flush reveal throws light straight at the back of your head from 6pm onwards in June and you will be redecorating the wall in September.

It is the single most valuable document in the business and it is the least protected.

The list is the product. The list must travel with the job. Everything else is logistics.

posts.hook: Five things that turn a good install into a bad one
posts.body:
1. The foam. Too little and it moves, too much and it bows the frame.
2. The fixings. Into the reveal, into solid, never into the old frame.
3. The gaps. If the perimeter gap is not consistent, the sealant tells the truth eventually.
4. The sill. Level, with fall, horned, and cut to the wall not to the paper.
5. The protection. If it isn’t taped, it will be marked. If it isn’t boarded, it will be scratched.

Five things. That is the craft.

posts.hook: The frame viewer made me realise how much glass we throw away
posts.body:
I made a thing that shows how much of a window is actually glass, from every angle, with the sightlines drawn in.

Then I looked at it for a very long time.

On a standard UK casement we are giving away 28% of the aperture to frame and bar. On a Georgian-barred box sash it is closer to 45%.

Once you see it you cannot unsee it. And you cannot unsee it in the customer’s sitting room either.

posts.hook: Foil or solid colour. The decision people get wrong.
posts.body:
Woodgrain foil looks fantastic for eleven years.

Then it lifts at a corner, or it fades in a south-facing bay, or somebody puts their kettle on the cill and it bubbles, and the window you specified is now a window you apologise for.

Solid colour is a different product with a different lead time and it is the only honest answer to a south-facing bay on a south-facing house.

posts.hook: “The last bloke did them all in two days.”
posts.body:
“The last bloke did them all in two days.”

The last bloke did them all in two days because the last bloke did not:

Foam them.
Scribe the reveals.
Get the cills to fall.
Shim them.
Tape the internal floors.
Board the stairs.

The last bloke did them all in two days and the house has a smell in it to this day. Nobody ever found out why. It was the foam.

posts.hook: Just one. And then the rest next year.
posts.body:
“Can you just do the front one for now and we’ll do the rest next year.”

Six months later the front one is fine and the back four are worse than the ones they replaced.

This is a real, lovely, human decision and it is the single most expensive thing a homeowner can do. You pay the survey, the mobilisation, the minimum order and the scaffold twice.

The entire job lives in that gap.

posts.hook: The five types of person at the front door
posts.body:
THE FIVE TYPES AT THE FRONT DOOR

1. The one who is certain it will be done next week.
2. The one who wants a price before you have even looked.
3. The one who will ask you to quote the whole street.
4. The one who wants to know if you do bathrooms.
5. The one who says “I’ll think about it” and is about to buy from whoever is cheapest.

And then, occasionally, type 6: the one who says “just tell me what you’d do.” Best customer in the world.

posts.hook: “Will it match the door?”
posts.body:
“Will it match the door?”

The door is composite. The door has no paint code. The door has been repainted once, badly, in a colour that used to be called ‘Magnolia’ and is now something else entirely.

You can get a colour match within about two years of the door being made if the door is in good condition. You cannot get it to match a composite door at all. Nobody can. The company that made it stopped making it in 2011.

And yet. We are all going to try.

posts.hook: What Article 4 actually does (in a way nobody explains it)
posts.body:
Slide 1: Normally, in England, replacing windows in a house is permitted development. No permission. Just do it.

Slide 2: Article 4 takes that right away from you in a specific direction — usually the front — usually to protect a view.

Slide 3: In a conservation area the same applies, and in Scotland since May 2024, prior notification applies to a lot of listed and street-facing windows.

Slide 4: On a listed building you need listed building consent and uPVC is basically never acceptable.

Slide 5: The mistake: finding out all of this after you have surveyed, specified and quoted.

posts.hook: The barn conversion nobody will pay for.
posts.body:
Change of use: agricultural barn to residential dwelling.

The planning gets granted. The building regulations get involved. The structural engineer says the roof needs work. The floor needs work. The wall insulation needs work. The moisture open-up of 1.2 metres into the gable end has to be coordinated with the fitter or the new window sits in a bucket.

Two years of work, one window in the middle of it, and the window is usually the only line the customer quotes out loud.

And the application to replace it reads: “REMOVAL OF THE CONSERVATORY TO FORM A SINGLE STOREY EXTENSION.”

Underneath that sentence is the easiest nine-window job in the county, because the shell is already there and the ground floor is already high.

Read the description. That is where the money is.

posts.hook: The non-material amendment. Free money, nobody uses it.
posts.body:
NON-MATERIAL AMENDMENT APPROVED.

That is the whole email. Six words. It means someone changed the spec slightly after approval and the council said yes.

A non-material amendment is a free, fast, low-stakes permission to change your window specification after the application was approved. A different colour. A different bar profile. A different glass.

Every one of those is a £40 item on a £900 window and it is the difference between winning the job and not. It takes one phone call. Almost nobody makes the call.

posts.hook: You cannot fit uPVC on a listed building. Full stop.
posts.body:
It has been said in every conservation officer’s letter in the country for thirty years.

A listed building gets timber or nothing. Slim-profile timber, matched to the original joinery, with a heritage justification written by somebody who has done it before.

It is harder. It is slower. It is better paid. And it is the job most window companies cannot be bothered to bid.

posts.hook: The 8-mile radius. Try 8 first.
posts.body:
Start at 8 miles.

Not 25. Not the county. Eight miles, twelve months, window and door work only.

Eight miles is an hour of driving, so it is a radius you can genuinely serve. Eight miles is small enough that you know every skip hire firm in it. Eight miles is large enough that there is work every week.

Then when you are consistently converting, go to 15. Then 25. Then open the second branch.

The radius is the whole strategy. Everything else is detail.

posts.hook: “The application is for the house next door.”
posts.body:
Every single person searching a planning portal finds this eventually.

The address is right. The description is right. The applicant is right. It is the wrong house, the wrong plot, or a house that does not exist yet, or a plot that was sold three times.

The map pins to the street rather than the property. The applicant field is a land registry placeholder. The plans are a site in Essex and the work is in Devon.

Check the plan, not the address. It takes ten seconds and it is the difference between a quote and an apology.

posts.hook: Where the margin actually goes
posts.body:
You did not lose that margin on the glass.

You lost it in the survey, when the opening was 9mm out and someone decided that would take a wedge.

You lost it in the office, when the fitting was never priced as a phase.

You lost it on the second visit, when the customer said “just while you’re here” and you went back.

You lost it on the delivery, when the frame was 2,180mm and went on two vans.

The factory is the only part of this where the numbers are honest.

posts.hook: The retrofit problem nobody prices
posts.body:
A new build window is a product.

A retrofit is an archaeology project with a frame at the end.

Hidden cavity, unknown wall build-up, a lintel that may or may not be structural, a previous owner who did something creative in 2004, a screed that will be in the way of the door swing, and a customer who has no idea any of this exists.

Price the survey properly and the job makes money. Skimp on the survey and it is a two-day job that takes five.

posts.hook: The five numbers a window business should actually run
posts.body:
Slide 1: Margin realised ÷ margin quoted. Anything under 0.85 is a problem.

Slide 2: Remakes ÷ units made. Over 2% is a fire.

Slide 3: Days enquiry to cash. Over 45 is a cashflow problem, not a sales problem.

Slide 4: Re-entries per job. Should be one. It is never one.

Slide 5: Quote-to-win rate. If it is under 25% you have a pricing problem, not a lead problem.

Five numbers. All from one record. All honest.

posts.hook: Stop calling it a survey. It is an investigation.
posts.body:
A survey is not someone pointing a tape at a hole.

A survey is: is this wall load-bearing. Where is the cavity. Why is there a pipe. Is the lintel original. Is that plaster load-bearing or is that 30mm of nothing. Is the reveal square. Is the cill going to be level. Is the render sound. Is the cavity wall insulated. Is the floor in the way. Is the socket in the wrong place.

And it is all captured in a way the office can actually use, the workshop can actually trust, and the installer can actually see on the day.

posts.hook: “We’re just a family firm.” You are a software company too.

Every person in this trade carries a small, bespoke, undocumented business logic in their head.

Rates. Supplier relationships. What a rough opening is worth. Which fitter to send. Which customer pays. Which job to do first. How much to apologise. When to walk away.

It is not written down. It is not tested. It is not backed up. It works right up until the day it is needed and cannot be found.

That is what software is: making the person in the head legible.

It is a systems thing. It is exactly and only a systems thing.

posts.hook: What 100 surveys taught me about UK houses
posts.body:
After a hundred surveys I can tell you these things with confidence:

The drawing is wrong more often than it is right.
The reveal is square about a third of the time.
The lintel is a problem roughly half the time.
Nobody has ever had the cavity filled correctly.
At least one window per job is above a downpipe.
The customer is right about the wall being level about four per cent of the time.

posts.hook: “Can we just…” is the most important sentence in product.

“Can we just put the survey on the phone?”

“Can we just have the quote come out with the drawing on it?”

“Can we just make the delivery wait until the balance is paid?”

“Can we just not retype the sizes?”

Every single good decision in this product came from a version of that sentence spoken by somebody in the trade who was annoyed on a Tuesday.

We are not designing software here. We are taking notes.

posts.hook: We are hiring. Here is the honest version.
posts.body:
We are looking for someone who has actually stood in a reveal.

Not a developer with a nice story about the trades. Someone who can look at a survey photo and say “that lintel is doing nothing, that cavity is full, and that trickle vent is in the wrong place” and then describe it in a sentence that a software developer can build from.

That person is worth more than another senior developer and they are much harder to find.

The office is the whole business and it is usually the quietest room in it.

Give a workshop those five things and it will run at 95% first-time-right without a single phone call.

Then take the phone away and give the sales team their morning back.

posts.hook: The most underrated person in a window business
posts.body:
Not the fitter. Not the salesperson. Not even the office.

The person who orders the glass and is right about the lead time.

That person knows that 24mm with a warm edge is nine days and 24mm standard is four. That person knows the uPVC is on holiday in August. That person knows to order the ironmongery before the frame arrives and not after.

That person is usually called Steve and is currently on a break.

posts.hook: The apprentice. Feed him properly.
posts.body:
The best thing you can do for an apprentice is to make him record the job properly.

Not the fitting. The job. The survey, the photos, the variations, the numbers, the materials. All of it, on a system, as he goes.

In three years he will not be an apprentice. He will be running jobs, pricing them properly, and not losing the information that everyone else loses.

And in five years you will have a manager, and you will not have had to train one.

A subcontract fitter who has to chase you for a drawing is a subcontract fitter who will do it slightly differently, on a slightly different day, and you will not find out until the customer mentions it.

Give them the job. Not a PDF of a job.

They see the same opening-by-opening record you see. Same sizes, same spec, same evidence, same conditions. They are part of the job, so the job should include them.

posts.hook: Myth: all double glazing is the same glass
posts.body:
Slide 1: There is a 2mm difference in cavity width, which is a 12% difference in energy loss.

Slide 2: There is argon and there is air, and it is about 15% of the U-value.

Slide 3: There is warm edge and there is aluminium, and it matters at the perimeter, which is where the loss actually is.

Slide 4: There is a coated face and there is a clear face, and it has to go the right way up or it is worse than nothing.

Slide 5: There is no such thing as a standard sealed unit. Ask for the make-up in millimetres and watch what happens.

posts.hook: Year end. The accounts do not fix themselves.
posts.body:
Year end is when everybody discovers the same thing at the same time.

The job that was quoted at forty per cent. The variation nobody invoiced. The retention nobody chased. The customer who paid in March. The skip hire in November that was still on an account that was closed.

None of this is a bookkeeping problem. It is a records problem, and it was a records problem in March.

posts.hook: The window industry has a data problem, not a sales problem
posts.body:
Nobody in UK window manufacturing is short of work.

What they are short of is certainty. Certainty about what was quoted. What was surveyed. What was ordered. What was made. What was delivered. What was paid.

Six organisations, six systems, and one person — usually the most overloaded person in the company — responsible for the integrity of the whole chain.

The remake rate in this industry is a direct, measurable function of how many systems a job passes through. It is not a quality problem. Quality is the best part of this trade. It is a reconciliation problem.

The fix is not better salespeople or better ads. It is one record that carries the specification, the price, the evidence and the history from enquiry to final invoice, written once and read everywhere.

It is not glamorous. It is the whole thing.

posts.hook: We built a job finder because nobody else bothered
posts.body:
There is a public register of every planning application in the United Kingdom. It is free. It is searchable. It contains, in plain English, what people are applying to build on specific addresses.

Roughly one in six of those applications includes window or door work worth quoting.

Almost nobody is using it. The reason is not a lack of access — it is that turning a PDF into a lead, and a lead into a survey, and a survey into a quote requires a person with a highlighter and a lot of free time.

We built it into the platform instead. Search by radius, by application type, by date. Flag conservation area, Article 4 and listed status. Estimate units and likely specification. Add it to the pipeline as a real record with the address and the works attached.

The interesting part is not the search. It is that the job arrives in the system already connected to surveying, configuring, quoting and delivery, so nobody has to rebuild it in six other tools.

If you install windows, this is a free, permanent, uncrowded pipeline in your own area. It has been sitting there the entire time.

posts.hook: Why we will not publish a customer testimonial
posts.body:
We could have a wall of them tomorrow. That was available to us on day one.

The reason we have not is that every customer we have is a window business, and a window business that publishes its own margin, its own remake rate and its own quoting failures to a software vendor's website has taken a risk it did not need to take.

So we will not ask.

What we will publish instead is four measures: time to quote, remakes, margin held against margin quoted, and re-entries per job. Real businesses, real figures, agreed in writing before anything goes on the site.

We have none of those published yet. Not because we do not track them, but because we do not have permission from the right number of people.

That is a slower way to build trust. It is also the only way that survives a reference call.

posts.body:
They lose it in four places that almost nobody writes down.

One: the survey. An opening comes in 9mm out, it becomes a wedge, a second visit and a morning, and it is absorbed because the quote was a lump sum with a fitting percentage buried inside it.

Two: the office. The specification is re-keyed between systems, and once it is re-keyed it belongs to whoever keyed it last.

Three: the second visit. “Just while you're here” has no scope, no price and no owner, and it is the single most expensive sentence in domestic construction.

Four: delivery. A 2,180mm frame on an unsuitable vehicle becomes two vans, and two vans are rarely in anybody's model.

None of this is a manufacturing problem. The manufacturing in this industry is genuinely world class.

It is a data problem, and data problems are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.

posts.hook: The spreadsheet is not a cheap version of quoting software
posts.body:
It is a shared, mutable document with no version history, no permissions, no validation and no relationship to anything else in the business.

Every modification overwrites the last. Two people cannot work in it at once. Nothing enforces that a width is a number. Nothing knows that opening W0.2 belongs to a survey that belongs to a job that belongs to a customer.

And the cell that somebody changed last Thursday — the one that moves a casement from 1200 to 1186 — has no record of who changed it, when, or why, and by the time anybody notices, the frame is on a van.

A spreadsheet is a genuinely useful tool. It is a terrible system of record.

The distinction matters because most small businesses have quietly decided that the spreadsheet is the system. It is not the system. It is the place the data goes to get lost.
